title: Pro's disaster 3-putt costs him full PGA Tour card
article_text:
We’re only halfway through the final PGA Tour event of the year, where players are fighting for PGA Tour status for next season. But the carnage is already apparent.

Look no further than the case of John Parry.

The 40-year-old entered the RSM Classic near the bubble for fully exempt PGA Tour status. On Friday, he was in line to make the cut and keep the fight going over the weekend, until a disastrous three-putt on his closing hole cost him the cut and, likely, his full PGA Tour card.

While there are a lot of permutations for PGA Tour status on the line at the RSM Classic, arguably the most impactful is the top-100 cutoff.

All players who finish within the top 100 of the FedEx Fall standings at the end of the tournament receive fully exempt status on the PGA Tour in 2027, as well as a spot in the Players Championship.

While that doesn’t necessarily mean they get access to next year’s Signature Events, at the very least, their playing schedules will be secure for a year, and they can play their way into the bigger events.

Parry is technically a rookie, having earned his 2026 PGA Tour card via the DP World Tour’s Race to Dubai last season. But he’s well aware of the top-100 cutoff.

Heading into the RSM Classic, Parry was stuck at 96th in the FedEx Fall standings. Though that’s not much of a cushion, the veteran pro would have likely needed only to make the cut at Sea Island to stay within the top 100.

Following an opening-round 70, Parry started Friday’s second round right on what would end up being the cut line: two under. A birdie at the Seaside Course’s second hole moved him to three under.

But then things got shaky. Parry made bogeys at 3 and 5, then two more at 13 and 14 to fall to one over. Incredibly, he then rallied with birdies at 15 and 17 to move back to one under.

As he headed to the 18th tee, the cut line still hovered at one under, meaning he only needed a par to play the weekend.

Parry striped his drive into the middle of the fairway, then knocked his approach to 29 feet. At the time, he believed a two-putt par would give him a made cut.

Unfortunately, he’d need more than two to finish out.

Parry’s birdie putt ran 3 feet, 10 inches past the hole. Then he lined up his par putt and pulled it just left of the hole, watching his ball nip the edge but fail to fall. A tap-in gave him a devastating bogey-5.

With his ugly finish, Parry had temporarily dropped to 99th in the FedEx Fall standings, which means he was still in line for a full PGA Tour card. But by round’s end, the cut line moved to two under, and Parry fell to 101st in the FedEx Fall standings.

There is some good news for Parry. Even though he likely won’t be fully exempt for 2027 as a result of his missed cut, he will still finish within the top 110, which will give him conditional PGA Tour status for next year and plenty of starts.

title: Haeran Ryu Opens With Bogey-Free 66 at CME Group Tour Championship
article_text:
Megan McCrea is the Manager of Digital Operations. Megan is in her second year with the LPGA, working with the LPGA and Epson Tours to manage, develop, maintain, and update website content.

NAPLES, Fla. — Haeran Ryu of the Republic of Korea carded a bogey-free 6-under 66 on Thursday to sit T4 after the first round of the CME Group Tour Championship, one shot behind co-leaders Jeeno Thitikul, A Lim Kim and Karis Davidson at Tiburón Golf Club.

The 25-year-old, who won the KPMG Women's PGA Championship and The Amundi Evian Championship in back-to-back starts this summer, closed with birdies on her final two holes to join eight other players at 6-under. The 66 is Ryu's lowest score in 13 career rounds at the season-ending event, where her previous best was a second-round 67 in 2025.

Thitikul, the two-time defending champion, A Lim Kim and Davidson each opened with 7-under 65s on the par-72 Gold Course, leaving a crowded leaderboard with three rounds to play.

Ryu started on the front nine and wasted no time, making birdie on the par-5 first hole to reach 1-under. She parred her next four holes before picking up another stroke at the par-5 sixth to move to 2-under, then added three more pars to turn in 2-under 34.

The back nine is where Ryu found another gear. After a par at the 10th, she birdied the par-4 11th to get to 3-under and followed with a birdie at the par-4 13th to climb to 4-under.

A run of three straight pars followed, including at the par-5 14th, the only par 5 she did not birdie on the day. Ryu then finished with a flourish, making back-to-back birdies at the par-5 17th and the par-4 18th to post an inward 32 and move within one shot of the lead.

In all, Ryu made six birdies and 12 pars, playing the four par 5s in 3-under and never dropping a shot.

Ryu credited a simple game plan for keeping a clean card, one that included taking cues from Thitikul, who has won this event each of the last two years.

“Today I just had two strategies on the golf course. First one, just not think about the golf course; just more control my swing,” said Ryu. “And second one is Jeeno is a pretty good player on this golf course, and I just wanted to follow her.”

Ryu admitted Florida has not always been kind to her. As a rookie in 2023, she tied for 36th in her first start at Tiburón.

“My first year I was a rookie, and Florida was not a good memory for me, so that’s why I need more experience on the golf course in Florida,” said Ryu. “But these days, way better than before.”

Ryu’s six-birdie effort continued a strong close to her season. She shot a 6-under 65 in difficult conditions on Saturday at The ANNIKA driven by Gainbridge at Pelican last week on her way to a T3 finish, and she was T2 at the BMW Ladies Championship in October.

It has been a breakthrough year for the 2023 Rolex Rookie of the Year. Ryu has 12 top-10 finishes in 17 starts in 2026 and has earned $4.9 million. She captured her first major title at the KPMG Women's PGA Championship at Hazeltine National Golf Club in June, then won The Amundi Evian Championship two weeks later in a playoff over Brooke Henderson. Her third-round 60 at Evian was the lowest score in LPGA major championship history.

Ryu entered the week third in the Race to CME Globe standings. She owns five career LPGA Tour titles: the 2023 Walmart NW Arkansas Championship, the 2024 FM Championship, the 2025 Black Desert Championship and her two 2026 majors.

This is Ryu's fourth appearance at the CME Group Tour Championship. She tied for 36th at 9-under as a rookie in 2023, tied for 35th at 6-under in 2024 and posted her best finish last year, a T10 at 13-under. Her previous opening rounds here were 69, 71 and 69 respectively.

With 54 holes remaining and a $4 million first prize on the line, Ryu is in position to add a third victory to her 2026 season. The path will not be easy. Twelve players are within one shot of the lead, and Race to CME Globe leader Nelly Korda opened with a 4-under 68 to sit T20.

Ryu said her approach for the rest of the week will not change.

“I just want to keep not thinking about the golf course and just want to keep patient in my swing,” said Ryu. “That’s it. Nothing more.”

Haeran tees off during second round of the CME Group Tour Championship at 11:55 a.m Friday.

title: Thitikul, Kim and Davidson share CME Group Tour Championship lead
article_text:
The LPGA Tour's season finale has a crowded leaderboard after the first day. Jeeno Thitikul, A Lim Kim and Karis Davidson each opened the CME Group Tour Championship at Tiburón Golf Club with a 7-under-par 65. They share the lead at -7, one stroke ahead of a nine-player group at -6. With three rounds still to play, very little separates the top of the 60-player field.

Thitikul is the most closely watched of the three co-leaders. The world No. 2 won this event in 2024 and 2025 and arrived in Naples trying to win the Tour Championship for a third year in a row. Her bogey-free-looking start of seven under puts her right in contention, although that bid is still three rounds away from being decided. A Lim Kim of South Korea and Karis Davidson of Australia matched her score, so the opening round produced a three-nation tie between Thailand, Korea and Australia.

Charley Hull is the best-known name in the group one shot back. The Englishwoman won this event in 2016 and shot a 6-under 66 that included seven birdies, missing only one fairway. She said she had struggled with her swing early in the round: "I felt like I had no swing feels. Then as the round developed, I hit it really nice." Looking back a decade, Hull joked: "It's crazy how long ago it was and how chubby I was back then." Her opening round continues a solid run of form: she has five consecutive top-25 finishes, including a tie for 17th at the previous week's event.

Eight other players are tied with Hull at -6, and Korea has the most of them. Hye Jin Choi, Somi Lee and Haeran Ryu all shot 66. So did Americans Lauren Coughlin, Jenny Bae and Auston Kim, Japan's Ayaka Furue and France's Pauline Roussin-Bouchard.

Another seven players are two shots off the lead at -5 after rounds of 67. They include Frenchwoman Celine Boutier and England's Lottie Woad, along with Australia's Grace Kim, Mexico's Gaby Lopez, Japan's Yuna Nishimura, American Yealimi Noh and China's Yan Liu.

The group at -4 is also within reach. It includes Spain's Carlota Ciganda, Australia's Hannah Green, Korea's Ina Yoon and Germany's Esther Henseleit. Henseleit's 68 leaves her three shots behind the leaders and in a good position to move up over the next three days.

Thirty players are within three strokes of the lead, so the opening round has settled very little. Low scores were common on Thursday, and anyone in the top 20 can expect to stay in contention with another good round. The second round on Friday should start to separate the field before the weekend. For now, Thitikul, Kim and Davidson are the players to catch, and a large group is close behind them.

title: LPGA Tour introduce ‘aggressive’ new solution to stop slow play
article_text:
The LPGA Tour is tackling pace of play head-on.

It's one of the biggest issues fans have with the modern game, as players are often taking around six hours to complete their rounds. And while the PGA Tour has often been criticized for not taking action to speed up the pace of play, the LPGA Tour is attempting to find solutions.

Their latest move is to fine any player who has been put on the clock over 35 times in a year $35,000. That's an extreme measure, considering the previous threshold was 40 holes, and the previous fine was $5,000.

Under the new policy, the maximum time allowed for a single shot also drops from 70 seconds to 60 seconds, and players will pay $2,000 for a first offense, $4,000 for a second, and $8,000 for a third.

Delays of six to 15 seconds still bring a one-stroke penalty plus a fine, while delays of 16 seconds or more carry a two-stroke penalty and a fine. LPGA Tour Commissioner Craig Kessler explained how the tour came to this new policy.

This new pace-of-play policy is a positive step for the LPGA Tour as it looks to speed up the game, and what's even more encouraging is that the players are also invested in fixing the issue.

How do we know that? Well, the players came up with the solution in the first place. That's according to Kessler, who said on SiriusXM Radio: "The good news is we started with our fans, and the insight from fans is that pace of play matters. Fans want to see us play faster. We brought that to our players, and we actually have a pace-of-play committee.

"And the beautiful thing here is it's the players who developed the policy. They're the ones that we understand the importance of playing faster. We understand what are the levers that we can pull to help bring that to life.

"And they're the ones who created the policy that we rolled out to frankly, a decent amount of applause from our players on Tuesday.

"I'm very excited to see the policy implemented. If it works as intended, fantastic, and of course if we need to learn and adapt as we go then we'll do just that."

This isn't the only step the LPGA Tour has taken. Unlike the PGA Tour, the LPGA has enforced two-stroke penalties on players this season, taking action on Yealimi Noh and Carlota Ciganda and ultimately costing them victories.

Kessler spoke about those instances: "There are two players this season that we have addressed two-stroke penalties to, and they actually lost the tournament on Sunday. And by the way, we didn't do it for that reason, but the reality is, when you've got a policy, if you want players to take that seriously, you have to enforce it.

"Those are tough calls, and sometimes leadership requires you to make unpopular decisions. But I'm proud of our rules team for sticking to the policy we put in place. And for what it's worth, you spend a minute on social and look at the fans' reaction, I think fans are very pleased to see how seriously we're taking this."

The fines likely won't translate into a punishment for the PGA Tour, as they would unfairly affect players who aren't making as much prize money week to week as the biggest stars.

But the PGA Tour can learn from how the LPGA Tour hits players where it hurts: their scorecard. They must follow suit and start docking shots for slow players.

title: Thitikul Stretches Tiburón Streak to Nine Straight Rounds in the 60s
article_text:
A Lim Kim has the lead at the CME Group Tour Championship. But the player behind her is the one who has owned Tiburón Golf Club for the past two years. Jeeno Thitikul has won this event in each of the last two years. On Friday in Naples, Florida, she shot 67 in the second round. That made it nine rounds in a row in the 60s for her at this course, and it keeps her in the race for a third straight title.

Thitikul is alone in second place at 12-under 132, three shots behind A Lim Kim. Kim leads at 15-under 129. Two rounds remain in the LPGA Tour's season finale, so the final weekend of the year now has a clear chase story.

Both players opened with 65 on Thursday. Kim then pulled ahead in the second round, and for a while it looked like she might get well clear. Thitikul answered late. According to golftoday.co.uk, she made five birdies over her last eight holes, which kept the gap to three shots heading into the weekend.

That kind of finish is nothing new for her here. The closing stretch from the 13th to the 18th has been one of her biggest strengths at Tiburón since 2024, and it played a big part in both of her titles. She finished strongly again on Friday, and those late birdies may well matter by Sunday afternoon.

Her run of nine straight rounds in the 60s tells the story of her record here. She does not just play this course well every so often. She shoots in the 60s almost every time she tees it up.

Thitikul still has a lot of ground to make up. Kim's second-round 64 gave her a 36-hole total of 129, the lowest score through two rounds at Tiburón since the event moved to the course in 2013. She birdied all four par-5s, and her round included a hole-in-one at the par-3 16th.

"I needed 155-yard shot, honestly a little strong hit and I make it," Kim said of the ace. "A little luck to me, yeah."

Luck may have helped at 16, but the rest of her round was simply very good golf. A three-shot lead over a two-time defending champion is a strong position. It is not a safe one, though, especially with Thitikul's record here.

The leaderboard is tight below the top two. Six players are tied for third at 11-under 133, just one shot behind Thitikul and four behind Kim:

That leaves Thitikul with a lot of company. If she has a quiet round, someone from that group could easily pass her.

Nelly Korda is at 9-under 135 after rounds of 68 and 67. She was bogey-free on Friday but still lost ground, going from three back after the first round to six back now. That shows how low the leaders went.

The question for Saturday and Sunday is simple. Can Thitikul's record at Tiburón beat Kim's form this week? If Thitikul keeps her streak going, Kim will need to keep scoring low to stay in front. If Kim's game holds up, Thitikul may need something special over the closing holes she knows so well.

Follow every shot on the CME Group Tour Championship leaderboard.

title: Gary Woodland Has Knee Surgery, Exits Hero World Challenge
article_text:
Woodland said he had been feeling discomfort in his knee and, after consulting with doctors, had the procedure Thursday night at the Hospital for Special Surgery in New York with Dr. Riley Williams, Golf Channel reported.

Keegan Bradley will take Woodland's place in the 20-player field as a tournament invite, Golf Channel and Golfweek reported. The event is Dec. 3-6 at Albany in the Bahamas.

Woodland had received his invitation Tuesday, along with tournament host Tiger Woods and Rickie Fowler, Golfweek reported.

title: Kim moves clear at LPGA finale after hole-in-one
article_text:
South Korea's A-Lim Kim aced the par-three 16th hole on her way to claiming a three-shot lead after the second round of CME Group Tour Championship.

The 31-year-old held a share of the lead after the first round at Tiburon Golf Club in Florida but is out on her own after shooting a superb 64 on Friday.

Kim made seven birdies and one eagle, the hole-in-one on 16, with a solitary bogey to head into the weekend 15 under and with a great chance of claiming the $4m (£3.05m) top prize.

"When I hit, after, I felt it was a little strong, but hit the pin and then went in," Kim said of her hole-in-one, the third of her career. "I think it was luck."

On the potential to win millions on Sunday, she added: "Money is money. It has not bothered me. I think winning is more important for me."

England's Charley Hull is one of six players four strokes back in a tie for third, with Jeeno Thitikul of Thailand one shot better off in second.

Hull posted a blemish-free 67, with five birdies, to keep herself right in the mix in a stacked field that contains the top 60 in this season's points list.

World number one Nelly Korda, who will qualify for the LPGA Hall of Fame if she wins on Sunday, also produced a five-under 67 and heads into round three tied for 11th on nine under.

With an $11m purse on offer, Korda would also break Annika Sorenstam's career earnings record if she finishes in sixth place or better.

The Swede amassed 10 major titles and earned $22,583,694 during a storied career before retiring in 2008, with Korda now just under $160,000 behind that mark.

title: LPGA Tour: Charley Hull in CME Group Tour Championship contention as A Lim Kim fires hole-in-one to grab halfway lead
article_text:
A Lim Kim fired a hole-in-one on her way to grabbing the halfway lead at the LPGA Tour's season-ending CME Group Tour Championship, where Charley Hull remains in contention.

Kim holed her tee shot with a seven iron at the 168-yard par-three 16th, with the Korean adding seven birdies and a lone bogey in a round-of-the-day 64 at Tiburon Golf Club.

The former US Women's Open champion was tied at the top of the leaderboard until her stunning ace and a birdie at the par-five next, which moved Kim to 15 under and three clear of back-to-back defending champion Jeeno Thitikul.

Thitikul posted five birdies in a seven-hole stretch on her back nine during a second-round 67, putting her in the final group on Saturday, with Hull a further shot back in a share of third after matching the world No 2's score.

Yuri Yoshida, Ina Yoon, Yan Liu, Jenny Bae and Auston Kim complete the logjam on 11 under alongside Hull, who posted five birdies in a blemish-free round as the 2016 champion looks to win the CME Group Tour Championship for a second time.

"I've just been pretty solid the last couple days, and hopefully I can replicate that on the weekend," Hull admitted. "I didn't actually hole that many putts, but I hit it quite close."

Only the top 60 players in the season-long Race to the CME Globe get to tee it up in Florida, with world No 1 Nelly Korda six off the halfway lead as she chase the $4m (£3.04m) winner's cheque.

"I'm just not hitting it as solid as I would like," Korda explained. "I have a little bit of a two-way miss going and that's kind of death for any golfer - you're not very confident over the shot.

"I'm just trying to get myself one key that I'm just going to go with for the whole week. I have yet to figure it out - hopefully the weekend brings me some luck!"

England's Lottie Woad dropped to tied-22nd after a two-under 70, while Ireland's Leona Maguire heads into the weekend sharing 42nd after rounds of 70 and 71 over the first two days.

title: PGA Tour blasts LIV Golf creditors over 'desperate fishing expedition'
article_text:
The PGA Tour has launched a strong response to a legal move by creditors involved in LIV Golf's bankruptcy proceedings, branding their attempt to obtain sensitive business records a "desperate fishing expedition".

The comments came after the official committee of unsecured creditors in LIV Golf's Chapter 11 bankruptcy case issued a subpoena to the PGA Tour on Friday, requesting documents across 18 separate categories.

The PGA Tour has been asked to provide the material by December 4, with the demands covering everything from its relationship with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) to financial information involving media rights, sponsorship agreements and player compensation.

However, the PGA Tour has made little secret of its frustration at being drawn into the proceedings.

"This document request is a desperate fishing expedition and a baseless attempt to try and drag the PGA Tour into the ongoing LIV Golf bankruptcy case," a Tour spokesperson told Front Office Sports.

"The efforts of these creditors should be dedicated towards LIV Golf and the parties responsible in the bankruptcy filing."

The latest development adds another twist to LIV Golf's increasingly complicated financial situation, following its November 5 announcement that it planned to wind down its operations.

Creditors have submitted more than $100 million in unsecured claims during the bankruptcy process, while LIV Golf has so far set aside $2 million for potential creditor recoveries, according to the information outlined in the proceedings.

The subpoena was filed by New Jersey-based law firm Fox Rothschild, representing the creditors committee alongside New York firm Willkie Farr & Gallagher.

Among the information being sought are documents connected to the previous litigation between the PGA Tour and LIV Golf, as well as communications concerning disciplinary action imposed or potentially considered against players who participated in, or explored joining, LIV events.

The creditors are also seeking records relating to the June 6, 2023 framework agreement involving the PGA Tour, DP World Tour and Saudi PIF.

Other areas of interest include communications concerning any arrangements or discussions that may have discouraged third parties from conducting business with LIV Golf, alongside documents connected to the US Department of Justice's inquiry into the proposed PGA Tour-PIF partnership.

Financial information is another significant part of the request, with the committee seeking details of the Tour's annual revenues, media-rights income, sponsorship earnings, tournament prize funds and overall player compensation.

Under bankruptcy legislation, creditors' committees have certain investigative powers allowing them to examine a debtor's financial affairs and business operations.

However, the subpoena does not automatically compel the PGA Tour to hand over every document requested. The organisation can challenge the demands or raise objections, potentially leaving the dispute to be considered by Judge Michael Kaplan, who is overseeing LIV Golf's bankruptcy case.

The next bankruptcy hearing is scheduled for November 24, with the latest dispute demonstrating that the fallout from LIV Golf's financial difficulties could extend well beyond the breakaway circuit itself.

title: PGA Tour: England's Marco Penge grabs halfway lead at RSM Classic as big names battle to secure FedExCup future
article_text:
England’s Marco Penge bolstered his hopes of retaining full status on the PGA Tour for next season by grabbing a share of the halfway lead at the RSM Classic.

Penge started the week 120th in the FedExCup standings and requiring at least a top-four finish to break inside the top 100 and guarantee full playing status on the PGA Tour in 2027.

A birdie-birdie finish saw Penge post a second-round 65 on the Stadium Course, one of two used at Sea Island Golf Club, leaving him in a four-way tie on nine under alongside Michael Thorbjornsen and Denmark's Rasmus Neergaard-Petersen.

"I'm in a bit of a weird situation," Penge admitted. "I missed seven or eight tournaments this year from injury and have some sort of medical exemption still, which I don't really know much about.

"I'm trying to feel like it's the last event, but at the same time knowing that I have maybe three or four, five tournaments to start next year that goes towards this year's ranking. There's a lot of us guys trying to keep our job this week and we're all trying to give it our all."

Thorbjornsen is already fully exempt on the PGA Tour next season, having won the Rocket Classic in August, while Neergaard-Petersen - like Penge - started the week outside the top 100 in the standings.

A congested leaderboard sees a further six players a shot back, including Ryder Cup player Rasmus Hojgaard as he looks to rise from 122 in the season standings, while England's Harry Hall heads into the weekend just two behind.

"It [FedExCup ranking] will always be in the back of your head a little bit," Hojgaard said. "There's still so much more golf to be played. I'm happy with the golf I played so far and hopefully I can keep doing that for the next few days."

Brooks Koepka, Presidents Cup star Jackson Koivun and past Ryder Cup captain Keegan Bradley are all four behind, while Christiaan Bezuidenhout - starting the week in 100th spot - is in tied-41st for the tournament and projected to drop down the standings.

A three-putt bogey on the final hole saw England's John Parry miss the cut by a shot, seeing him currently projected to finish in 101st spot, while eight-time PGA Tour winner Billy Horschel played his last three shots in four over and also made an early exit.

Those 51st to 60th after this week qualify for the first two Signature Events of 2027, while those who end between 101st and 125th on the PGA Tour only receive conditional status and be unable to feature in certain events.

Players outside the top 125 face a season on the Korn Ferry Tour or a trip to Q-School to earn their PGA Tour playing rights, with first-round leader Svensson entering the week in 135th spot.
